No prior paper explicitly reframes the cause of "Brain Rot" degradation during continual pretraining (CPT) on short-sequence data. None of the prior papers establish or reframe this specific problem.

### Mechanism
The mechanism — controlled experiments attributing "Brain Rot" to per-token weight disparity caused by short sequences receiving disproportionately high per-token gradient updates — is not covered by any prior paper. Papers like [19] ("Why Gradients Rapidly Increase Near the End of Training") and [17] ("Spike No More") analyze gradient-related phenomena but focus on different contexts, such as late-stage training spikes or gradient norm stabilization. [11] ("MixGradient") and [20] ("Gradient-aware learning for joint biases") discuss gradient re-weighting schemes for imbalanced data streams but do not address per-token weight disparity due to sequence length. No prior paper identifies or experimentally attributes degradation to this specific mechanism.

The evaluation measures an 8.17x per-token gradient/weight disparity as the causal mechanism. Papers like [19] ("Why Gradients Rapidly Increase Near the End of Training") and [17] ("Spike No More") analyze gradient norms but do not use the same evaluation design or protocol to measure per-token weight disparity. Similarly, [13] ("Token-level Fitting Issues of Seq2seq Models") discusses token-level phenomena but does not measure gradient disparities in the same way. No prior paper employs this specific evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain — continual pretraining of large language models on short-sequence corpora — is covered by [16] ("Sequence Length is a Domain"), which explicitly addresses length-based overfitting in transformer models during training. Additionally, [28] ("Batch-level Experience Replay with Review for Continual Learning") discusses continual learning methods, albeit in computer vision, and [7] ("COCO-LM") addresses pretraining challenges for language models. While these papers do not target the exact sub-problem of "Brain Rot" or short-sequence degradation, they operate within the same general application area of continual pretraining for large language models.
